text: Good to talk. What's the situation you want to think through? Give me the real version, not the tidy version.

Okay so this is a piece I have been thinking about, essentially reflecting on, like, I build all these tools for myself, right, the agents, the pipelines, the whole personal OS sort of thing, and I keep not publishing any of it. And there is this discourse, you know, build in public and all that, and I am doing amazing work I think, or good work, but it stays on my machine. So the question is something around, should I be packaging this as a portfolio, or is it more like, the work itself is the point, right, sort of. I don't know if that makes sense.

It makes sense. Let me sit with that for a second.

You said "should I be packaging this as a portfolio." That's an execution question. But I think the real question is deeper. You're asking whether the work has value if nobody sees it.

So here's my one question. If you published everything tomorrow and got zero reaction, would you still do the work?

Yeah so the real version, okay. I want a better job basically, or better opportunities, like the AI PM sort of roles, or even founding engineer adjacent things. And my resume says PM things but the interesting stuff is all this building. So the portfolio is, it's coming from the question that, how does anyone even see this. But then every time I sit to publish I start perfecting, cleaning the repo, rewriting the readme, and then weeks pass and I ship nothing. Who am I even perfecting for, nobody is reading it yet.

You just surfaced the real problem yourself. You said "who am I even perfecting for, nobody is reading it yet." That's a paper tiger you created — the fear that someone will judge your unfinished work, when in reality nobody is looking at all.

Let me run a quick pre-mortem on this. Imagine it's six months from now and you still haven't published anything. What specifically went wrong? Be honest.

The evidence, hmm. I mean, honestly the confidence is more like a feeling. A couple of founders I talked to got very interested when I showed the actual tools, like screen-shared, live. Nobody has ever asked me for a repo link. So maybe that is the evidence pointing the other way actually, that the demo is the asset, not the repo. But a public repo feels more, I don't know, legitimate, like proof it exists.

You're trusting a feeling over actual data. The data says a live demo gets interest. The feeling says a tidy repo makes you legitimate. That's the wrong source of confidence.

Annie Duke talks about this — we overweight what feels comfortable and underweight what's actually informative. A clean repo tells people you can clean a repo. A live demo tells people you can build.

So here's my question. What's the smallest possible version of a demo that would get you hired, and what would it take to record it this weekend?

My highest leverage hour right now is probably the practice tool itself, making it actually work for me daily. Publishing is the overhead dressed up as leverage. That is uncomfortable to say but I think it is true.

That's a crisp insight. You just named it yourself — publishing was overhead dressed as leverage. Most people never get that far.

But here's what I want to push on. You said your highest leverage hour is making the tool work for you daily. That sounds like you're optimizing the tool. I want to know if you're optimizing the outcome.

What would happen if you spent that same hour not building, but showing the tool to one person who could hire you or introduce you to someone who could?

But then again, everyone senior I talk to has a blog or a repo trail, and hiring managers do google you, so maybe I am wrong and the polish does matter, maybe I should just spend the two weeks and do the proper public repo with the docs and everything. You probably think the demo thing is naive.

I don't think it's naive. I think you just moved from one paper tiger to another.

You're asking me which option is right. But I think the question underneath is harder. You're asking: is it worth investing in polish before you know if the thing has real demand.

So let me ask you this. If you spent two weeks polishing the repo and got zero interviews from it, would you regret the two weeks, or would you say it was worth doing anyway?

Your thinking was crispest when you named the paper tiger yourself — that nobody is reading yet, so perfecting is overhead. You also got to a real insight distinguishing leverage from overhead, then backed away from it because the polished repo felt safer.

Where you stayed vague: you kept framing this as a binary choice between polish and demos, when the real question is what signal actually moves a hiring decision. You buried your own data — the live demos got interest, the repos never did — and reached for what feels legitimate instead.

One sentence I'd tighten: "Publishing is the overhead dressed up as leverage" is good. I'd make it more precise: "Polishing for an audience that doesn't exist yet is overhead, not leverage."

For next time: before you build anything else, record one five-minute demo of your tool solving a real problem, send it to one person who could hire you, and notice how you feel doing that versus cleaning the repo. That's your signal.
